full_judgment:
2. The Rule in Writ Petition Number 11518 of 2017 was issued challenging order dated 25-4-2016 passed by the Additional District Judge, Bankruptcy Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case Number 3 of 2011 (arising out of Bankruptcy Case Number 37 of 2002) striking out the name of the respondents number 3-10 from the plaint of the bankruptcy case and cancelling the gazette published with their names, if any, while similar order dated 19-4-2016 passed by the same court in Miscellaneous Case Number 1 of 2010 (arising out of Bankniptcy Case Number 46 of 2002) was challenged in Writ Petition. Number 11519 of 2017. 

 3. The petitioner Pubali Bank Limited lent money against two loan accounts of respondent number 2 in both the writ petitions. As he failed to make repayment, the creditor-bank served statutory notice and instituted two separate bankruptcy cases against the principal borrower as defendant number 2 and the guarantors, who were impleaded as defendants number 3 to 4 and the then manager of the concerned branch was made defendant number 5 in both the bankruptcy cases. 

 4. During pendency of the cases, one of the guarantors Kamal Uddin died and the creditor-bank substituted him by his legal heirs and successors (respondents number 3 to 9 herein). Ultimately the cases were allowed and the defendants were declared bankrupt by two separate judgment and orders one dated 12-5-2004 and another dated 23-5-2004 (Annexure-C to both the writ petitions). The matter was in fact pending for publication in gazette. At that stage, defendant number 4 Salauddin, who stood as a guarantor against the loan filed two separate applications for restoration of the bankruptcy cases on setting aside the ex-parte judgment and orders dated 12-5-2004 and 23-5-2004. The applications were registered as Miscellaneous Cases Number 1 of 2010 in Bankruptcy Case Number 46 of 2002 and Miscellaneous Case Number 3 of 2011 in Bankruptcy Case Number 37 of 2002. Both the miscellaneous cases were long delayed. 

 5. Learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court took up the miscellaneous cases, heard the parties and rejected the same by two separate orders dated 19-4-2016 and 25-4-2016. Learned Judge-rejected the miscellaneous cases on the ground that according to rule 32 of the Bankruptcy Rules, 1997; such an. application could be filed within 15 days. Learned Judge, however, suo motu corrected its previous orders dated 12-5-2004 and 23-5-2004 on the ground that there was an apparent mistake in declaring the guarantor and heirs of the guarantor, namely, defendants number 3(Ka)-3(Chha) and 4 as banknipts, and struck out their names from the plaint of the bankruptcy cases and cancelled the gazette published in their names, if any. 

 7. Mr Md Nazmul  Hoque , learned advocate for the petitioner submits that as soon as the learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court passed the original judgment and orders, he became functus officio and was no more competent to change any material part of the order. In the present case, notices were duly served upon all the defendants, but they did not appear and contest the bankruptcy cases. After passing the judgment and order, one of them appeared with a delayed restoration application, which was rightly rejected. But the learned Judge committed serious mistakes in striking out the names of the defendant number 4 and the heirs of defendant number 3. 

 8. Mr  Hoque  refers to section 5 (Chha) of the Bank Companies Act and further submits that by legal definition, the guarantor is also a loanee and M case of his failure in fulfilling the formal demand made under section 9(1)(Jha) and 9 (2.) of the Act, 1997, he is liable to be impleaded in the bankruptcy case. Learned judge of the Bankruptcy Court rightly allowed the bankruptcy cases and declared them bankrupts. Learned Judge, however, after disposal of the case, sat on his own judgment and reviewed the same by way of correction, which was out and out illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 9. In support of his submission, Mr Hoque refers to the case of Mokbul Hossain Mridha and others vs Md Shamsul Huq Sarder and others 64 DLR (AD) 97 and Emdadul Haque Bhuiyan vs The Court of District .Judge and Bankruptcy Court, Narayangonj and others 2001 BL D (AD) 119. 

 10. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocate and gone through the record. In the case of Mokbui Hossain Mridha as cited by Mr Hoque, the High Court Division after making the Rule absolute in a civil revision, recalled its judgment and made the Rule absolute on merit. The Appellate Division on a certificated appeal reversed the judgment of the High Court Division holding that after passing the judgment on merit, the High Court Division became functus officio. In the cited case, the original suit was for declaration of title over a piece of land, not for declaration of bankruptcy under the Bankruptcy Act. In the present case, learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court did not change the ultimate judgment and order declaring the principal borrower a bankrupt, but made correction thereto by deleting the names of the heirs of a deceased guarantor [defendants number 3(1(a)—(Chha)] and that of defendant number 4, which he was legally authorized to do under sections 110 and H1 of the Act, 1997. 

 11. In the case of Emdadul Haque Bhuiyan, as relied on by the learned advocate for the petitioner, the guarantor-defendant filed an application praying for dismissal of the plaint under section 28(b) of the Act, 1997. It means that he had sufficient ability to pay off the loan as a parantor. As he could not prima-facie prove his ability, the application was rejected and the original order of rejection was upheld up to the Appellate Division. The basic question, whether he was liable to be declared a bankrupt was not the issue before the trial court. It was also not argued in the cited case that any provision like section 6(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is not available in the Bankruptcy Act, 1997. In the cited case, if the application was allowed, the principal borrower could also escape the liability of repaying the loan. But in the present case, only the heirs of the guarantor and another guarantor himself were struck out from the plaint and excluded from the gazette, if already published. So, distinction is apparent between the cited cases and the case in hand. 

 12. The purpose of Bankruptcy Act, 1997 and that of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and the Bank Companies Act, 1991 are quite different. The purpose of Ain, 2003 is realization of loan from the defaulting borrower. The Ain in its section 6(5) clearly speaks of impleading the guarantor as defendant in the suit thereunder. In case of failure of the principal judgment debtor after decreeing an artharin suit, a guarantor-debtor is also liable to repay the money and can be proceeded in an execution case. Whereas, the purpose of Bankruptcy Act is to discourage nonpayment of loan to a bank or an individual, and to curtail some civil and political rights of the citizen, who had taken loan and enjoyed the same, but did not repay its creditor. Although in different laws including the Bank Companies Act, both the defaulting borrower and guarantor against a defaulted loan are defined as debtor, they are not equal in all cases. A guarantor is a person who does not enjoy the loan money, but helps another in taking loan and takes the risk of- being proceeded against, when the original borrower fails to repay. That is the reason the Bankruptcy Act does not include a guarantor in its sections 9 and 10. So the moral and legal status of a guarantor and bonower in the Bankruptcy Act is not the same as in the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and the Bank Companies Act. The harsher law i.e. the Ain, 2003 in its section 34(4) prohibits civil imprisonment of the heirs of a deceased debtor. 

 13. In a case, where the loanee dies keeping the loan unpaid, the creditor can at best sue his legal heirs and successors for recovery of money from his Estate/Property, which the heirs and successors inherit from him. But in other cases, there is no scope to curtail the political and civil rights of a citizen because of any wrong committed by his predecessor. 

 14. Learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court in passing the original orders dated 12-5-2004 and 23-5-2.004 had committed mistakes in decreeing the case against the legal heirs and successors of defendant number 3 Kamal Uddin, and also against defendant number 4 Salauddin, who were guarantors against the loan taken by defendant number 2. Sections 110 and I 1 l of the Bankruptcy Act confer authority on a Bankruptcy Court to rectify and correct its own judgment, in excise of which learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court passed the impugned orders. 

 15. Learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court in passing the impugned orders also relied on the case of Kill Akhtaruzzaman Agrani Bank and others 57 DL R 57, where the legal provisions of Bankruptcy Act have been discussed and the guarantors have been excluded from the scope of being adjudged as bankrupt. In taking such view, Md Abdul Latin, J as his lordship was then) observed: 

 "8. This liability according to us is a liability with regard to the payment of the money and if for that payment guarantor stands surety he has the notice of the consequence of non-payment by the principal debtor. But the Bankruptcy Act of 1997 is a special law which has created a special liability and therefore, this special law must be construed very strictly and unless the guarantor is brought within the definition of the word debtor specifically the guarantor cannot be saddled with the liability for being adjudged as bankrupt. Absence of the word guarantor in section 10 indicates that it was not the intention of the legislature to saddle the guarantor with the additional liability of being adjudged as bankrupt. Whenever an offence or a liability is created by law it is specifically provided in the Jaw and cannot be inferred unless it is created by law against the guarantor. The court has no power to rewrite the law and in that case it will be an act of judicial legislation which is not permitted by law."
